about: The concept index of milestone 10: twenty-five Platonic concepts, each with the Greek words it is indexed under, Plato's own passages, the ancient and later definitions, the later Platonists' readings, and its relations to the others. Every link quotes the words it rests on, and the build looks for each quotation in the text it names (reports/concepts.md). Nothing is linked because two passages share a word: shared words are shown apart, as lexical evidence, and notes that name a concept are shown apart, as found by rule. The 'note' of each concept is the index's own sentence on what is gathered under it, not a definition.

sources.plato: Burnet's Greek, at the Stephanus section named.
sources.taylor-terms: Thomas Taylor, 'Explanation of Certain Platonic Terms', The Works of Plato vol. I (1804); texts/taylor-1804/vol1/platonic-terms.json.
sources.definitions-hermann: The Definitions (Ὅροι) printed with Plato's works, not by Plato; Hermann's Greek (OCR).
sources.definitions-burges: The same Definitions in Burges' English (1854, OCR).
sources.alcinous-burges: Alcinous, the handbook of Platonic doctrine (2nd century AD), in Burges' English (1854, OCR), by Burges' chapters.
sources.note: A note in the library: a commentator's or translator's note, at the work and section named.

layers.plato: Plato names it and argues about it in the dialogues.
layers.plato-later: Plato names it; its systematic form (its place in an order of principles) is the later Platonists'.
layers.later: A doctrine of the later Platonists. Plato does not name it; the passages listed are those the later readers cite or read it from, and are marked so.

concepts.label: The Good
concepts.note: The Good as Plato speaks of it (the form of the Good, 'beyond being' in the Republic) and as the later Platonists identify it with the first principle.

terms.note: the adjective, and τὸ ἀγαθόν, 'the good', which GLAUx tags under it; most occurrences are ordinary 'good'.

definitions.quote: τὸ αὑτοῦ ἕνεκεν
definitions.says: The Definitions: the good is 'that which is for its own sake'.

definitions.quote: Good—the cause of safety to things existing
definitions.says: The Definitions, a second definition, in Burges' English.

passages.quote: ἡ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἰδέα μέγιστον μάθημα
passages.why: Socrates calls the form of the Good the greatest study.

passages.quote: τὴν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἰδέαν φάθι εἶναι
passages.why: The Good as the cause of knowledge and truth, like the sun of sight.
The Good 'beyond being' (ousia) in dignity and power.

passages.quote: ἐν τῷ γνωστῷ τελευταία ἡ τοῦ
passages.why: At the end of the ascent from the cave, last and hardest to see.
The Philebus: the good is complete and sufficient, and all that knows it pursues it.

later.quote: he has laid down our good in the knowledge and contemplation of the primary good, which a person would call god and the primary mind
later.says: Alcinous identifies the primary good with god and the first mind.

later.quote: The good itself is prior to being
later.says: Proclus: the good is prior to being.

evidence.quote: αἰτίαν δʼ ἐπιστήμης οὖσαν καὶ ἀληθείας

related.why: The Good is the cause of knowledge and truth.
The Good is beyond being.
The Definitions define the beautiful as the good.
The maker of the cosmos was good.

concepts.label: The Beautiful
concepts.note: Beauty itself, the goal of the ascent of love in the Symposium, and beauty seen through the senses in the Phaedrus.

terms.note: 'beautiful, fine, noble'; most occurrences are ordinary praise.

definitions.quote: Καλὸν τὸ ἀγαθόν
definitions.says: The Definitions: the beautiful is the good.

passages.why: Diotima: beauty itself always is, neither coming to be nor passing away.

passages.quote: τὰ δὲ ἄλλα πάντα καλὰ ἐκείνου μετέχοντα
passages.why: All other beautiful things share in it.
The ascent by steps to beauty itself.
The Phaedrus: of the forms beauty alone shines clearly through sight.
The Phaedo: a thing is beautiful because it shares in the beautiful itself.

later.quote: and a beautiful thing, Tbecause he is (so) by himself more than that by nature and symmetrical
later.says: Alcinous names the first god beautiful (the OCR's 'T' is a note mark).

related.why: Beautiful things share in beauty itself.
The ascent of love ends in it.

concepts.label: Truth
concepts.note: Truth as what the Good gives to what is known, the 'plain of truth' the soul sees, and truth in speech and belief.

definitions.quote: ἕξις ἐν καταφάσει καὶ ἀποφάσει
definitions.says: The Definitions: truth is a state in affirming and denying.

definitions.quote: Truth—a habit in affirming and denying; a knowledge of things true
definitions.says: The same, in Burges' English.

definitions.quote: Plato, following ancient theologists. considers truth multifariously
definitions.says: Taylor: truth is spoken of in many ways, the highest being the light from the good.

passages.quote: τὸ τὴν ἀλήθειαν παρέχον τοῖς γιγνωσκομένοις
passages.why: The Good gives truth to what is known.
The souls strive to see the plain of truth.
As being is to becoming, so truth is to belief.

later.quote: and truth, because he is the beginning of all truth, as the Sun is of all light
later.says: Alcinous: the first god is the beginning of truth.

evidence.quote: αἰτίαν δʼ ἐπιστήμης οὖσαν καὶ ἀληθείας

related.why: Knowledge and truth both come from the Good.
Truth stands to belief as being to becoming.

concepts.label: Being
concepts.note: What always is and never comes to be, set against what comes to be, and being as one of the greatest kinds in the Sophist.

terms.note: 'being, substance, essence'; also 'property' in the ordinary sense.
'to be': τὸ ὄν, 'what is', is tagged under it. Very broad: almost every occurrence is the ordinary verb.

definitions.quote: the first principle or foundation, as it were, of the essence of a thing
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Hyparxis: the summit of essence.

passages.quote: τί τὸ ὂν ἀεί, γένεσιν δὲ οὐκ ἔχον
passages.why: Timaeus' first distinction: what always is and has no becoming.
The Phaedo: being itself, always the same.

passages.quote: τὸ μὲν παντελῶς ὂν παντελῶς γνωστόν
passages.why: What wholly is, is wholly knowable.

passages.quote: τὴν οὐσίαν δὴ κατὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦτον γιγνωσκομένην
passages.why: The Sophist: being as known, and whether it is moved.

later.quote: although desirous to lay hold of the Being, yet are they in a dream
later.says: Alcinous on the sciences that dream of being.

evidence.quote: τί τὸ ὂν ἀεί, γένεσιν δὲ οὐκ ἔχον, καὶ τί τὸ γιγνόμενον μὲν

related.why: The first division of the Timaeus.
What wholly is, is wholly knowable.

concepts.label: Becoming
concepts.note: What always comes to be and never is, grasped by opinion with sensation; generation.

terms.note: 'to become, come to be'. Very broad.

definitions.quote: Γένεσις κίνησις εἰς οὐσίαν
definitions.says: The Definitions: becoming is a motion towards being.

definitions.quote: Generation—a movement towards existence
definitions.says: The same, in Burges' English.

definitions.quote: A flowing condition of being, or a subsistence in becoming to be
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Generation, from Proclus on the Timaeus.

passages.quote: δόξῃ μετʼ αἰσθήσεως ἀλόγου δοξαστόν, γιγνόμενον καὶ ἀπολλύμενον
passages.why: What becomes is grasped by opinion with sensation.
The Theaetetus: the view that nothing ever is, but always becomes.

later.quote: Fables call the ineffable unfolding into light through causes, generation
later.says: Taylor, quoting Proclus on the Parmenides: 'generation' in the myths means the procession from causes.

related.why: What becomes never really is.
Becoming is grasped by opinion and sense.
Becoming is the object of opinion.

concepts.label: The Forms
concepts.note: The forms (ideas): one in each case, by themselves, in which the many things share.

definitions.quote: Now persons define Idea as the eternal pattern of things existing according to Nature
definitions.says: Alcinous: the Idea is the eternal pattern of natural things.

passages.why: The Phaedo: each of the forms is something.
Each form is one, but appears many.

passages.quote: εἶδος γάρ πού τι ἓν ἕκαστον
passages.why: One form for each set of many things with one name.

passages.quote: χωρὶς μὲν εἴδη αὐτὰ ἄττα, χωρὶς δὲ τὰ τούτων αὖ μετέχοντα
passages.why: Parmenides questions Socrates on which things have forms.

passages.quote: ἀναίσθητα ὑφʼ ἡμῶν εἴδη, νοούμενα μόνον
passages.why: The Timaeus: forms not sensed, only thought.

later.quote: Now Idea is, as regards god, a mental operation by him; as regards us, the first thing perceptible by mind
later.says: Alcinous: the Ideas are the thoughts of god.

later.quote: For it does not please the majority of Platonists (to admit) that there are Ideas of works of art
later.says: Alcinous on which things have Ideas.

evidence.quote: ἤτοι ὅλου τοῦ εἴδους ἢ μέρους ἕκαστον τὸ μεταλαμβάνον μεταλαμβάνει

related.why: Parmenides asks how things share in a form.
Each form is one but appears as many.
The forms are only thought.
The craftsman makes looking to the form.

concepts.label: Intellect (Nous)
concepts.note: Intellect: in the cosmos (the world-soul's intellect, intellect as king of heaven and earth) and in us; for the later Platonists, the second principle.

terms.note: νοῦς: GLAUx files it under its uncontracted form νόος.

definitions.quote: In the human soul is the summit of dianoia
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Intellect: in us the summit of discursive reason; in divine natures an eternal essence perceiving all at once.

definitions.quote: Νόησις ἀρχὴ ἐπιστήμης
definitions.says: The Definitions: intellection is the beginning of knowledge.

passages.why: The Timaeus: intellect cannot come to be in anything apart from soul.
The Philebus: the wise agree that intellect is king of heaven and earth.
Socrates on Anaxagoras: intellect orders all things.
The Laws: soul with intellect guides all things rightly.

later.quote: this would be the primary god, as being the cause %of perpetually operating for the mind of the whole heaven
later.says: Alcinous: the first god, a mind, causes the activity of the mind of heaven.

evidence.quote: νοῦν δʼ αὖ χωρὶς ψυχῆς ἀδύνατον

related.why: Intellect needs soul to be in a body.
Intellection is the beginning of knowledge.

concepts.label: Reason and Logos
concepts.note: Logos as account, argument and reason; reasoning (logismos); thought as the soul's dialogue with itself.

terms.note: 'word, speech, account, argument, reason, ratio': many meanings, most of them ordinary.

definitions.quote: This word in Platonic writers signifies either that inward discursive energy called reasoning; or a certain productive and seminal principle; or that which is indicative and definitive of a thing
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Reason: three senses of logos.

definitions.quote: When applied to divinity as by Plato, in the Timæus, signifies a distributive cause of things
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Logismos.

passages.why: Socrates' 'second sailing': taking refuge in accounts (logoi).
The Sophist: thought and speech are the same, thought being the soul's silent dialogue.
The Theaetetus: is knowledge true opinion with an account?
What always is, is grasped by intellection with an account.

later.quote: Productive principles or powers; and they also signify forms
later.says: Taylor, s.v. Reasons (logoi), from Proclus on the Timaeus.

later.quote: But reason likewise is a judge, through which the truth is judged
later.says: Alcinous: reason as the judge of truth.

evidence.quote: δόξα ἀληθὴς οὔτε μετʼ ἀληθοῦς δόξης λόγος προσγιγνόμενος ἐπιστήμη ἂν εἴη

related.why: The Theaetetus ends: knowledge is not true opinion with an account.
Being is grasped by thought with an account.

concepts.label: Soul (Psychē)
concepts.note: Soul: self-moving and immortal, the world-soul of the Timaeus, the parts of the soul in the Republic.

definitions.quote: Ψυχὴ τὸ αὐτὸ ἑαυτὸ κινοῦν
definitions.says: The Definitions: soul is what moves itself.

definitions.quote: that which moves itself
definitions.says: The same, in Burges' English.

passages.why: The Phaedrus: all soul is immortal, being self-moving.
The Laws: soul is the motion that moves itself.
The Timaeus: the world-soul, best of things begotten.
The Republic: the soul in its truest nature.

later.quote: That the soul is immortal (Plato) proves by proceeding in this
later.says: Alcinous gathers Plato's arguments for immortality.

later.quote: It is plain then that the World is a thing of life and intellectual
later.says: Alcinous on the world-soul.

related.why: Soul guides rightly when it takes intellect to itself.

evidence.quote: Moreover if learning is (but) recollection, the soul would be immortal

related.why: Alcinous: recollection shows the soul immortal.

concepts.label: The Demiurge
concepts.note: The maker and father of the cosmos in the Timaeus, good and without envy, who looks to the eternal pattern; for the later Platonists a rank among the gods.

terms.note: 'craftsman'; in the Timaeus the maker of the cosmos. Most occurrences elsewhere are ordinary craftsmen.
'maker, poet': the Timaeus' 'maker and father'. Mostly 'poet'.

definitions.quote: The artificer (maker) of the universe is thus denominated, because he produces the universe so far as it is a whole
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Demiurgus of Wholes.

passages.why: The maker and father of this universe, hard to find and impossible to declare to all.
The maker is good and looked to the eternal pattern.
He was good, and without envy wished all things to be like himself.
His speech to the gods he has made.
The Statesman: the world remembers the teaching of its maker and father.
The Republic: the craftsman of the heavens.

later.quote: Jupiter, the artificer of the universe
later.says: Taylor, s.v. Demiurgus: the Neoplatonists' Jupiter.

later.quote: the perpetuity of the universe is suspended from the goodness of its maker
later.says: Proclus on the goodness of the maker.

related.why: He was good.

evidence.quote: ὁ δημιουργὸς πρὸς τὸ κατὰ ταὐτὰ ἔχον βλέπων ἀεί

related.why: He makes looking to what is always the same, as to a pattern.
He put intellect in soul and soul in body.

concepts.label: The One and the Many
concepts.note: The one and the many in the Philebus and the Parmenides; for the later Platonists the One is the first principle, read from the Parmenides' hypotheses.

terms.note: 'one'; τὸ ἕν, 'the one', is tagged under it. Very broad.

definitions.quote: in divine natures is that which contains distinct, but at the same time profoundly-united multitude
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Monad.

definitions.quote: In a way conformable to the nature of The One
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Unically.

passages.why: The Philebus: the one and the many in every account.
The Parmenides: the first hypothesis, if the one is.
The second hypothesis, if one is.

later.quote: The first procession therefore from the first cause will be the Intelligible triad
later.says: Taylor on the order of principles read from the Parmenides.

related.why: Each form is one.

concepts.label: Participation
concepts.note: Things share (metechein, metalambanein) in the forms, and Parmenides' questions about how they share.

definitions.quote: That which is not consubsistent with an inferior nature
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Imparticipable: the later doctrine of what is not shared in.

passages.why: Beautiful because it shares in the beautiful itself.

passages.quote: ἢ ἄλλη τις ἂν μετάληψις χωρὶς τούτων γένοιτο
passages.why: Parmenides: does each share in the whole form or a part?
Beautiful things share in beauty itself, which is not changed by it.

later.quote: he conceived to have obtained that appellation from their participating somehow in the primary and most honoured (good)
later.says: Alcinous: goods are so named by sharing in the first good.

later.quote: is a God through participation, and not on account of its own proper essence
later.says: Proclus: what is good by participation, as against what is good of itself.

related.why: Sharing in the form.

evidence.quote: their participating somehow in the primary and most honoured (good)

related.why: Alcinous: all goods share in the first good.

concepts.label: Emanation (procession)
concepts.note: The procession of all things from the first principle, which Taylor renders 'progression' and 'procession'. Not a word of Plato's: the passages are the ones the later Platonists read it in.

definitions.quote: Fables call the ineffable unfolding into light through causes, generation
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Generation, quoting Proclus.

passages.quote: πάντα ὅτι μάλιστα ἐβουλήθη γενέσθαι παραπλήσια ἑαυτῷ
passages.why: Read by Proclus as the procession of all things from the goodness of the maker.

read_by.quote: For the procession of the Gods frum the principle of all things

passages.why: Read by Taylor (after Proclus) as the first procession from the first cause.

read_by.quote: The first procession therefore from the first cause will be the Intelligible triad

later.quote: we conceive of the nature of things in a two-fold respect, either according to their progression, or according to their conversion
later.says: Proclus: things are seen by their progression and their conversion.

evidence.quote: either according to their progression, or according to their conversion

related.why: Procession and return (conversion) go together in Proclus.

evidence.quote: the perpetuity of the universe is suspended from the goodness of its maker

related.why: Proclus: the universe depends on the goodness of its maker.

concepts.label: Return (conversion)
concepts.note: The return or conversion (epistrophē) of what proceeds back to its source. Plato's word for the soul's turning is periagōgē; the systematic doctrine is the later Platonists'.

terms.note: 'turning around', the soul's turning in the Republic.

definitions.quote: Restitution to a pristine form, or condition of being
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Apocatastasis.

definitions.quote: That which elevates the soul from sensibles to intelligibles
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. the Anagogic.

passages.why: Education is an art of turning the soul around, from becoming to being.

later.quote: For that which returns, is made as it were that which abides
later.says: Proclus: what returns becomes like what abides.

later.quote: as abiding, proceeding, and returning
later.says: Taylor from Proclus: abiding, proceeding and returning.

related.why: The turning of the soul begins its ascent.

evidence.quote: either according to their progression, or according to their conversion

related.why: Procession and conversion together.

concepts.label: Knowledge
concepts.note: Knowledge (epistēmē) as against opinion, its objects, and the Theaetetus' search for what it is.

definitions.quote: Ἐπιστήμη ὑπόληψις ψυχῆς ἀμετάπτωτος ὑπὸ λόγου
definitions.says: The Definitions: knowledge is a conception of the soul not to be overturned by argument.

definitions.quote: Knowledge—a comprehension by the soul
definitions.says: The same, in Burges' English.

definitions.quote: This word is sometimes defined by Plato to be that which assigns the causes of things
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Science.

passages.why: The Theaetetus asks what knowledge is.

passages.quote: ἐπʼ ἄλλῳ ἄρα τέτακται δόξα καὶ ἐπʼ ἄλλῳ ἐπιστήμη
passages.why: Knowledge and opinion are set over different things.
The Meno: true opinions become knowledge when tied down by reasoning about the cause.
The Theaetetus ends without a definition.

later.quote: of which the one, conversant about things perceptible by mind, is Science and Scientific Reason
later.says: Alcinous: science is of the intelligible.

evidence.quote: ἐπʼ ἄλλῳ ἄρα τέτακται δόξα καὶ ἐπʼ ἄλλῳ ἐπιστήμη

related.why: Different powers, over different things.
Tying down by the cause is recollection.
The Meno: if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it can be taught.

concepts.label: Opinion
concepts.note: Opinion (doxa), true and false, between knowledge and ignorance, and its object, what becomes.

definitions.quote: Is the last of the gnostic powers of the rational soul
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Opinion: it knows that a thing is, not why.

definitions.quote: This power knows the universal in particulars
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Doxastic.

passages.quote: οὔτε ἄρα ἄγνοια οὔτε γνῶσις δόξα ἂν εἴη
passages.why: Opinion is neither ignorance nor knowledge, but between.
True opinions run away from the soul unless tied down.

passages.quote: εἰ μὲν νοῦς καὶ δόξα ἀληθής ἐστον δύο γένη
passages.why: The Timaeus: if intellect and true opinion are two kinds, there are forms.

later.quote: Now this is called Opinion through our combining the recollection brought previously into action with the sensation recently produced
later.says: Alcinous: opinion joins memory to fresh sensation.

evidence.quote: τὸ μὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν διὰ διδαχῆς, τὸ δʼ ὑπὸ πειθοῦς ἡμῖν ἐγγίγνεται

related.why: One comes by teaching, the other by persuasion.

evidence.quote: οὔτε ἄρα ἄγνοια οὔτε γνῶσις δόξα ἂν εἴη

related.why: Opinion lies between.

concepts.label: Ignorance
concepts.note: Ignorance, and the worst kind of it, thinking one knows what one does not.

terms.note: 'lack of learning, stupidity'; in the Sophist, thinking one knows.

definitions.quote: so far as it is ignorance, and a privation of science
definitions.says: Taylor: ignorance is a privation of science.

passages.quote: τὸ μὴ κατειδότα τι δοκεῖν εἰδέναι
passages.why: The Sophist: thinking one knows what one does not, called stupidity (amathia).
The Apology: Socrates is wiser only in not thinking he knows.

passages.quote: μὴ ὄντι μὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀπέδομεν
passages.why: Ignorance is set over what is not.

evidence.quote: οὔτε ἄρα ἄγνοια οὔτε γνῶσις δόξα ἂν εἴη

related.why: Opinion is between knowledge and ignorance.
Taylor: ignorance is a privation.

concepts.label: Virtue
concepts.note: Virtue (aretē): whether it is knowledge and can be taught, the virtues of the soul, and true virtue with wisdom.

definitions.quote: διάθεσις ἡ βελτίστη
definitions.says: The Definitions: virtue is the best disposition.

definitions.quote: a (mental) constitution of the best kind
definitions.says: The same, in Burges' English.

passages.why: The Meno: if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it can be taught.
The Phaedo: true virtue is with wisdom.
The Republic: the soul cannot do its work without its own excellence.

later.quote: While Virtue is a thing divine
later.says: Alcinous: virtue is divine, the best constitution of the soul.

evidence.quote: καὶ ἀνδρεία καὶ σωφροσύνη καὶ δικαιοσύνη

related.why: Justice is among the virtues.
Whether virtue is knowledge.

concepts.label: Justice
concepts.note: Justice in the city and in the soul: each part doing its own.

definitions.quote: Δικαιοσύνη ὁμόνοια τῆς ψυχῆς πρὸς αὑτήν
definitions.says: The Definitions: justice is the soul's agreement with itself.

definitions.quote: an agreement of the soul with itself
definitions.says: The same, in Burges' English.

passages.why: Justice is doing one's own.
The just man harmonizes the three parts of his soul.
Justice is to the soul as health to the body.

later.quote: But Justice is a certain agreement
later.says: Alcinous: justice is the three parts' agreement.

evidence.quote: καὶ δικαιοσύνη καὶ συλλήβδην ἀληθὴς ἀρετή

related.why: One of the virtues.
Justice is a state of the soul.

concepts.label: Evil as privation
concepts.note: Evil as a lack or failure of good, the later Platonists' doctrine. Plato says that god is not the cause of evils and that evil must always be opposed to the good; the doctrine of privation is Proclus' and Taylor's reading.

definitions.quote: a deviation from sub sistence, eitherthrou^h a privation of symmetry
definitions.says: Proclus: evil comes about by a deviation from being, a privation of symmetry (OCR as received).

passages.quote: τῶν δὲ κακῶν ἄλλʼ ἄττα δεῖ ζητεῖν τὰ αἴτια, ἀλλʼ οὐ τὸν θεόν
passages.why: God is not the cause of evils.

passages.quote: ὑπεναντίον γάρ τι τῷ ἀγαθῷ ἀεὶ εἶναι ἀνάγκη
passages.why: Evils cannot perish: there must always be something opposed to the good.

passages.quote: ἀγαθὰ μὲν πάντα, φλαῦρον δὲ μηδὲν εἶναι κατὰ δύναμιν
passages.why: The god wished all things good and nothing bad, so far as possible.

read_by.quote: But it subsists in the privation of symmetry

later.quote: that which is most distant from thr good is evil itself
later.says: Proclus: what is furthest from the good is evil itself (OCR 'thr').

evidence.quote: ὑπεναντίον γάρ τι τῷ ἀγαθῷ ἀεὶ εἶναι ἀνάγκη

related.why: Something must always be opposed to the good.
Taylor: ignorance is a privation.

concepts.label: Image and original
concepts.note: The cosmos as an image of its pattern, time as a moving image of eternity, the images of the divided line, and likenesses and semblances.

definitions.quote: A pattern, or that with reference to which a thing is made
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Paradigm.

definitions.quote: A thing is said to subsist iconically, when it subsists after the manner of an image
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. Iconically.

passages.quote: τόνδε τὸν κόσμον εἰκόνα τινὸς εἶναι
passages.why: This cosmos must be an image of something.

passages.quote: εἰκὼ δʼ ἐπενόει κινητόν τινα αἰῶνος ποιῆσαι
passages.why: Time, a moving image of eternity.
The divided line: images and what they are images of.
The Sophist: likeness-making and semblance-making.

later.quote: the image, as it were, of eternity
later.says: Alcinous: time the image of eternity.

evidence.quote: περί τε εἰκόνος καὶ περὶ τοῦ παραδείγματος αὐτῆς

related.why: The image and its pattern.

evidence.quote: τόνδε τὸν κόσμον εἰκόνα τινὸς εἶναι

related.why: The visible cosmos is an image.

concepts.label: Ascent
concepts.note: The soul's going up: out of the cave to the intelligible, and by steps to beauty itself; and becoming like god.

definitions.quote: That which elevates the soul from sensibles to intelligibles
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. the Anagogic.

passages.quote: τὴν εἰς τὸν νοητὸν τόπον τῆς ψυχῆς ἄνοδον
passages.why: The way up out of the cave is the soul's ascent to the intelligible.
The ascent of love by steps.

passages.quote: φυγὴ δὲ ὁμοίωσις θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν
passages.why: Flight from here is becoming like god, as far as possible.
The soul that once looked up to what truly is.

later.quote: one is an ascent from things perceptible by a sense to the primary perceptible by mind
later.says: Alcinous: analysis as an ascent to the intelligible.

related.why: The ascent is to the intelligible place.

evidence.quote: ἐν τῷ γνωστῷ τελευταία ἡ τοῦ

related.why: Last in the knowable is the form of the Good.

concepts.label: The intelligible world
concepts.note: The intelligible (what is grasped by thought), the 'intelligible place' of the Republic, ruled by the Good.

definitions.quote: This word in Plato and Platonic writers has a various signification
definitions.says: Taylor, s.v. the Intelligible: three senses.

passages.why: The Good rules in the intelligible place as the sun in the visible.

passages.quote: τὸ μὲν νοητοῦ γένους τε καὶ τόπου
passages.why: Two kinds, the visible and the intelligible.
The intelligibles that always are.

later.quote: there will have been the primaries perceived by mind, and the primaries perceived by a sense
later.says: Alcinous: primary intelligibles and primary sensibles.

related.why: The two kinds.

evidence.quote: ἔν τε νοητῷ αὐτὴ κυρία ἀλήθειαν καὶ νοῦν παρασχομένη

related.why: In the intelligible the Good is sovereign.

concepts.label: The sensible world
concepts.note: The visible and sensible: what becomes and is grasped by opinion with sensation.

passages.why: The visible and the intelligible.
Sensibles are grasped by opinion with sensation.
The Phaedo: what can be touched and seen, and what only reasoning grasps.

later.quote: the other, conversant about things perceptible by a sense, is Opinionative and Opinion
later.says: Alcinous: opinion is of sensibles.

related.why: Sensibles come to be.
Grasped by opinion.

concepts.label: Recollection
concepts.note: Learning as recollection of what the soul knew before birth.

definitions.quote: Μνήμη διάθεσις ψυχῆς φυλακτικὴ τῆς ἐν αὐτῇ ὑπαρχούσης ἀληθείας
definitions.says: The Definitions, of memory: a disposition of the soul that keeps the truth in it.

passages.quote: τὸ γὰρ ζητεῖν ἄρα καὶ τὸ μανθάνειν ἀνάμνησις ὅλον ἐστίν
passages.why: The Meno: seeking and learning are all recollection.
The Phaedo: learning is recollection, so the soul was before.

passages.quote: τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶν ἀνάμνησις ἐκείνων ἅ ποτʼ εἶδεν ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ
passages.why: The Phaedrus: recollection of what the soul once saw with god.

later.quote: for learning could not be based otherwise than on the recollection of what has been known of old
later.says: Alcinous on recollection.

evidence.quote: ἡ μάθησις οὐκ ἄλλο τι ἢ ἀνάμνησις τυγχάνει οὖσα

related.why: Cebes: if learning is recollection, the soul existed before.

evidence.quote: τοῦτο δʼ ἐστίν, ὦ Μένων ἑταῖρε, ἀνάμνησις

related.why: Tying down true opinions by reasoning is recollection.
